sentences.text: Knoetschkesuchus is a small atoposaurid crocodylomorph, a group of reptiles related to crocodiles, distinguished by having only two distinct types of teeth and lacking the leaf-shaped teeth found in other members of its family.

The species K. guimarotae reached a maximum length of 55 centimeters, while both species possessed long, slender limbs and two rows of bony, rectangular osteoderms on their backs that were wider than they were long.

The genus Knoetschkesuchus was formally described by Schwarz and colleagues in 2017, containing two species: the type species K. langenbergensis and K. guimarotae, which was originally classified as Theriosuchus guimarotae.

Specimens of K. langenbergensis, including a juvenile skull and a partial skeleton with osteoderms, were preliminarily described in a 2006 paper before being re-examined with a stereo microscope and formally named in 2017 by Daniela Schwarz, Maik Raddatz, and Oliver Wings.

The species K. guimarotae originates from the Guimarota quarry near Leiria, Portugal, a site dating to the Kimmeridgian stage when Europe consisted of scattered archipelagos surrounded by the shallow inland Tethys Ocean.
Knoetschkesuchus primarily fed on small prey such as invertebrates, amphibians, and mammals, though some specimens show evidence of having been scavenged by other animals.

Phylogenetic analyses consistently show that Atoposauridae, represented by Knoetschkesuchus, Theriosuchus, and Alligatorium, forms a monophyletic clade, and strongly support a close relationship between K. langenbergensis and K. guimarotae, excluding other Theriosuchus species.

The deposits containing K. langenbergensis date to the Upper Kimmeridgian stage of the Jurassic and are part of the Lower Saxony Basin, associated with the Rhenisch, Bohemian, and London-Brabant Massifs, while the Guimarota strata containing K. guimarotae have been dated to the Kimmeridgian based on fossil ostracods.

Researchers noted that the nasal bones completely divide the nostrils in Knoetschkesuchus, a trait not seen in the genus Theriosuchus, suggesting a distinction between them, and Schwarz et al. cited the fact that K. langenbergensis differs in four out of nine traits from the Theriosuchus diagnosis as a basis for separating it into the genus Knoetschkesuchus and revising the diagnosis, although some researchers previously attributed specimens of K. langenbergensis to another species of Theriosuchus, T. pusillus.
